title: Business Analytics with Power BI
tagline: Learn the part of Power BI that decides whether the numbers are right: the model and DAX, with a live DAX window in your browser
summary: Learn Power BI the way it is really built: a clean star-schema model, measures in DAX, and reports that people can read. Every DAX lesson and lab has a live DAX window that evaluates your measures on a real model in a matrix like Power BI's, with filter context, CALCULATE, relationships and time intelligence. Power BI Desktop itself is a Windows application and does not run in a browser, so the Power Query, report-design and Service lessons are explained with scenarios and checked with sorting and writing activities.

modules.title: Power BI and the BI workflow
modules.summary: See what business intelligence is for, how Power BI's parts fit together, how data gets in, and how Power Query prepares it.
modules.outcome: You can describe the Power BI components and the BI workflow, choose between Import and DirectQuery, and explain what Power Query steps and query folding do.
modules.intro: Business intelligence (BI) turns data into decisions people can see: a sales dashboard a manager opens every Monday, a report that shows why a number moved. Power BI is Microsoft's BI tool, and it is built around a simple pipeline: get data, shape it, model it, visualise it, share it. This course teaches the middle of that pipeline in depth, the data model and the DAX language that makes a report intelligent, because that is where reports are made right or wrong. One honest note up front: Power BI Desktop is a Windows application, so the report-building steps in this course are explained and shown rather than run in your browser. What does run here is the DAX: the practice window evaluates your measures on a model, in a matrix like Power BI's.

topics.title: What Power BI is, and its parts
topics.html:
Power BI is a family of tools, not one program. Knowing which part does what saves a lot of confusion.

The Power BI family
PartWhat it isTypical use
Power BI DesktopA free Windows applicationConnect to data, shape it, build the model and the report
Power BI ServiceThe online site (app.powerbi.com)Publish, share, schedule refresh, collaborate, build dashboards
Power BI MobileApps for phones and tabletsView and interact with reports on the move
Power BI Report BuilderA separate desktop toolPaginated (print-ready) reports
Power BI Report ServerAn on-premises serverOrganisations that must keep reports inside their own network

The semantic model (the new name for what was called a dataset) is the heart: the tables, relationships and measures that many reports can share. A good model means a new report takes minutes and every report gives the same numbers; a bad one means every report needs its own fixes.

Definition

Semantic model. The data tables, relationships, calculations (measures) and settings behind a report. One model can feed many reports.

Worked example

Who does what in a small team

A retailer's BI workflow.

  1. An analyst builds the model and report in Desktop and publishes it to a workspace in the Service.
  2. The Service refreshes the data every morning.
  3. Store managers open the report on their phones; the finance lead builds a second report from the same model.

Answer. Build the model once and reuse it. That is the single biggest time saver in Power BI.

Watch out

Several screens in this course are described rather than run, because they need the desktop app. Where that is so, the lesson says so, and the practice windows that do run (DAX) check that you understand the idea.

Tip

When you meet a new Power BI term, ask: is it about data (Power Query), the model, calculation (DAX), presentation (the report) or sharing (the Service)? Sorting terms this way makes the product much less confusing.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking Power BI is only a charting tool. Most of the skill is in the model and the measures.
  • Building a separate copy of the data for every report.
  • Skipping the model and putting everything in one huge flat table.
Try it yourself: Which part would you use to share a finished report with colleagues?

Model answer. The Power BI Service: publish the report from Desktop to a workspace, then share it or publish an app.

Check what you just learned

1. Where do you build the data model and the report?
  • Power BI Mobile
  • Power BI Desktop (correct)
  • The browser only
  • Excel

Desktop is the authoring tool.

2. A semantic model is:
  • A chart
  • A colour theme
  • The tables, relationships and measures behind reports (correct)
  • A phone app

It is the shared foundation.
keyPoints: Desktop builds, the Service shares, Mobile views, Report Builder makes paginated reports.
The workflow is get, transform, model, visualise, share.
A semantic model is built once and reused by many reports.

topics.title: Getting data: connectors and storage modes
topics.html:
Power BI connects to hundreds of sources through connectors: Excel and CSV files, folders, SQL databases, SharePoint, web APIs, cloud services. The first real decision is how the data is stored once connected.

Storage modes
ModeHow it worksGood forWatch out
ImportData is copied into Power BI's compressed in-memory engineSpeed; the full set of DAX and Power Query featuresData is as old as the last refresh; size limits
DirectQueryNothing is copied; each visual sends a query to the source when you view itVery large data; always-current dataSlower; some features limited; load on the source
Live connectionConnect to a model that already exists elsewhereReusing one governed modelYou cannot change the model
CompositeMix of Import and DirectQuery tables in one modelLarge facts plus small imported lookupsMore complex to design

Import is the default choice. It is fast because Power BI's engine stores each column compressed in memory, and it supports everything. Choose DirectQuery only when the data is too big to import or must be current to the minute.

Worked example

Choosing a mode

A sales table has 8 million rows and finance reviews it weekly.

  1. Eight million rows compress well: Import is usually fine.
  2. Weekly review does not need live data: a scheduled refresh each morning is enough.
  3. Import is faster for users and supports full DAX.

Answer. Reach for DirectQuery when you must, not by default.

Habits when connecting

  • Connect to the cleanest, most stable source available (a database view rather than a hand-edited spreadsheet).
  • Bring in only the columns and rows you need; every extra column costs memory.
  • Use a parameter for a folder path or server name so the report moves between test and production.
  • Keep credentials out of the file: Power BI stores them securely with the data source.
Watch out

Hand-edited spreadsheets are the fragile link in many reports: someone adds a column, renames a header or leaves a blank row, and the refresh fails. Connect to a controlled source whenever you can.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing DirectQuery 'to stay live' for data that changes once a day.
  • Importing every column of a wide table.
  • Pointing a report at a file on a personal computer.
Try it yourself: Which storage mode is the default, and why?

Model answer. Import: it is fast and supports the full feature set; the data is refreshed on a schedule.

Check what you just learned

1. Which mode copies the data into Power BI?
  • DirectQuery
  • None
  • Live connection
  • Import (correct)

Import loads a compressed copy.

2. DirectQuery is best when:
  • Data is too big to import or must be current (correct)
  • Data is tiny
  • You want faster visuals
  • You use Excel files

It trades speed for freshness and scale.
keyPoints: Connectors bring data in; Import copies it into a fast in-memory engine.
DirectQuery queries the source live: for huge or always-current data only.
Bring in only what you need and prefer controlled sources.

topics.title: Power Query: preparing data with repeatable steps
topics.html:
Power Query (the Transform data window) is where you clean and reshape data before it reaches the model. Every action you take becomes a recorded, editable applied step, written in a language called M. Refreshing the report replays all the steps on the latest data.

Common transformations
TaskPower Query command
Remove unwanted columnsChoose Columns / Remove Columns
Fix types (text, number, date)Data Type (set it explicitly)
Clean textTransform → Format → Trim, Clean, Capitalize
Split 'Pune, 411001'Split Column → By Delimiter
Months in columns to rowsTransform → Unpivot Columns
Summarise before loadingGroup By
Stack two tablesAppend Queries
Look up from another tableMerge Queries (a join)
Remove blanks and duplicatesRemove Rows
Worked example

A tidy-up in five steps

A monthly sales file arrives with a title row, months as column headings and prices stored as text.

  1. Use First Row as Headers, after removing the title row.
  2. Select the Product column and choose Unpivot Other Columns: months become rows.
  3. Set Month to a date type and Amount to a decimal type.
  4. Remove blank rows.
  5. Rename the columns clearly and Close & Apply.

Answer. Next month's file goes through the same five steps automatically.

Definition

Query folding. When Power Query translates your steps into a single query the source database runs itself (for example SQL), so the filtering and grouping happen at the source and only the result travels to Power BI. Steps that fold are fast; one step that cannot fold may force everything after it to run locally.

Watch out

Do the steps that reduce data (filter rows, remove columns) early, so they can fold to the source. A late filter after a step that breaks folding can mean Power BI downloads everything first.

This course's browser practice does not run Power Query: it needs Power BI Desktop. The cleaning ideas are the same as in the Excel and Python courses: trim, set types, unpivot, remove blanks and duplicates, and record what you did. If you understand those, you understand Power Query.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving columns as the wrong type, which breaks relationships and totals later.
  • Editing values by hand in the query instead of fixing the rule.
  • Merging queries on columns with different types or stray spaces.
Try it yourself: Which command turns month columns into rows?

Model answer. Unpivot Columns (or Unpivot Other Columns).

Check what you just learned

1. What is an applied step?
  • A chart
  • A recorded transformation that is replayed on refresh (correct)
  • A DAX measure
  • A workspace

Power Query records every action.

2. Query folding means:
  • Folding a report
  • Compressing a file
  • Power Query's steps run as one query at the data source (correct)
  • Merging two charts

The source does the work.

Key terms: flip and sort

Power BI Desktop
The authoring application for models and reports.
Power BI Service
The online site for publishing and sharing.
Semantic model
The tables, relationships and measures behind reports.
Import
Data copied into Power BI's in-memory engine.
DirectQuery
Each visual queries the source live.
Applied step
A recorded Power Query transformation.
Query folding
Steps run at the source as one query.
keyPoints: Power Query records cleaning as applied steps (written in M) that refresh replays.
Filter and remove columns early so steps can fold to the source.
Set data types explicitly and keep the cleaning rule-based.

modules.title: Data modelling: the star schema
modules.summary: Design a model that gives correct answers: facts and dimensions, relationships and filter direction, and a date table.
modules.outcome: You can split data into fact and dimension tables, set up relationships with the right cardinality and direction, build and mark a date table, and explain how a filter flows through a model.
modules.intro: If you remember one thing from this course, make it this: the model is more important than the report. Almost every wrong number in a Power BI report traces back to the model: a missing relationship, a table that is a flat copy of everything, a missing date table. The good news is that there is one pattern that works nearly everywhere, the star schema, and once you see how filters flow through it, DAX becomes far easier to understand. The practice windows use a small star schema, so you can watch filters flow.

topics.title: Facts, dimensions and the star schema
topics.html:
A star schema has one central fact table surrounded by dimension tables, joined like the points of a star.

Fact versus dimension
Fact tableDimension table
HoldsEvents or transactions: each sale, each click, each shipmentDescriptions of the things involved: products, stores, dates, customers
RowsMany (thousands to billions)Fewer (tens to millions)
ColumnsKeys to dimensions, and numbers to add up (quantity, amount)A unique key, and descriptive attributes (name, category, region)
ExampleSalesProducts, Stores, Dates

Filters flow from the 'one' side to the 'many' side. Select the category 'Home' in the Products table and Power BI keeps only the Sales rows for Home products; select the region 'North' in Stores and only North's sales remain. You never write a join: the relationship does it.

Watch a filter flow through the model

Run it: the measure adds up Sales[Amount], and the matrix splits it by a column of the Products table. Then change the visual to 'Sales by region' to see the Stores table filter the same facts.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Worked example

Why not one big flat table?

A flat table repeats the product name, category, store name and region on every sale row.

  1. Fix a typo in a category name and you must change thousands of rows.
  2. The model is larger and slower, because repeated text takes memory.
  3. Different questions need different lists (all products, even ones not sold), and a flat table cannot provide them.

Answer. A star schema stores each fact once and is smaller, faster and easier to change.

Watch out

A snowflake (a dimension that links to another dimension) is allowed but adds hops and complexity. Prefer to flatten dimensions into one table each unless there is a reason.

Common mistakes

  • One giant table with everything in it.
  • Using a fact table's own columns (product name text) to slice instead of the dimension.
  • Several fact tables joined directly to each other instead of through shared dimensions.
Try it yourself: In the model above, which table is the fact table?

Model answer. Sales: it holds one row per sale and the numbers to add up. Products, Stores and Dates describe the sales.

Check what you just learned

1. Which table in a sales model is the fact table?
  • Products
  • Stores
  • Dates
  • Sales (correct)

It holds one row per sale and the numbers.

2. Filters flow:
  • From the one side to the many side (correct)
  • From many to one
  • Both ways always
  • Nowhere

A filter on a dimension reaches the fact table.
keyPoints: A star schema has a central fact table and dimension tables around it.
Facts hold numbers and keys; dimensions hold descriptions and a unique key.
Filters flow from the one side (dimension) to the many side (fact).

topics.title: Relationships: cardinality, direction and keys
topics.html:
A relationship connects a column in one table to a column in another. Three properties matter.

Relationship properties
PropertyOptionsRule of thumb
CardinalityOne-to-many (dimension to fact), one-to-one, many-to-manyUse one-to-many. Avoid many-to-many unless you understand the consequences.
Cross-filter directionSingle (one to many) or BothKeep Single. 'Both' can create ambiguity and slow reports; use it rarely and deliberately.
ActiveOne active relationship between two tables; others inactiveInactive ones are switched on inside a measure (with USERELATIONSHIP).

What makes a good key

  • Unique on the one side (a product id appears once in Products).
  • The same data type on both sides.
  • A surrogate key or an id, not a name that might be spelled two ways.
  • Present in the dimension for every value in the fact (otherwise facts fall into a '(Blank)' group).
Worked example

An orphaned key

A sale refers to ProductID 'P9', but the Products table has no P9.

  1. The sale still counts in the grand total.
  2. When you slice by Product, it appears under '(Blank)'.
  3. Totals by product then do not add up to the grand total unless you show the blank group.

Answer. Check for facts without a matching dimension row; fixing it at the source is better than hiding the blank.

Watch out

Many-to-many relationships and two-way filters are the usual cause of 'the numbers are wrong but I cannot see why' reports. The default pattern, single direction one-to-many from each dimension, is simple and predictable.

Role-playing dimensions. A sales table might have an order date and a ship date, both related to one Dates table. Only one relationship can be active; the other is inactive and used in measures with USERELATIONSHIP. The practice engine here covers the core idea (one active relationship) and does not run USERELATIONSHIP, which the Desktop does.

Common mistakes

  • Relating tables on a name column that has duplicates.
  • Mismatched data types (text on one side, number on the other), which silently match nothing.
  • Turning on two-way filtering to 'make it work'.
Try it yourself: What cardinality and direction should a Products-to-Sales relationship have?

Model answer. One-to-many (one product, many sales), with a single filter direction from Products to Sales.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is the recommended relationship setup?
  • Many-to-many, both directions
  • One-to-many, single direction (correct)
  • One-to-one everywhere
  • No relationships

It is simple and predictable.

2. A sale whose key is missing from the dimension appears under:
  • The first product
  • Nothing at all
  • (Blank) (correct)
  • A new product

Orphaned facts group under blank.
keyPoints: Use one-to-many relationships with single-direction filters.
Keys must be unique on the one side, the same type on both, and present in the dimension.
Check for orphaned keys; avoid many-to-many and two-way filters unless needed.

topics.title: The date table and model hygiene
topics.html:
Time intelligence (year to date, same period last year) needs a proper date table: a table with one row per day, with no gaps, covering every date in your data, marked as the model's date table.

A date table
DateYearMonthNumMonthQuarter
2024-01-0120241JanQ1
2024-01-0220241JanQ1
……………
2025-12-31202512DecQ4

Date table rules

  • One row per day, no gaps, from before the first sale to after the last.
  • A unique Date column, with no times.
  • Mark it as the date table (Table tools → Mark as date table) so time intelligence works correctly.
  • Relate its Date column to the date column of each fact table.
  • Add Year, Quarter, Month and MonthNum, and sort Month by MonthNum so months appear Jan to Dec, not alphabetically.

Dates filter the facts too

The Dates table filters Sales by year. Try the visual 'Category by year', and change SUM to COUNTROWS(Sales) to count sales instead.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Watch out

The 'Auto date/time' feature creates hidden date tables for every date column. It is convenient for one-off reports but bloats the model; switch it off and use one proper date table.

Model hygiene checklist

  • Hide columns users should not drag into visuals: foreign keys, helper columns.
  • Name tables and columns for humans (Total Sales, not col_ttl_sls).
  • Remove columns you will never use: they cost memory.
  • Set data types and formats (currency, percentage, no decimals for counts).
  • Put measures in one place and format them.
  • Use the star schema and one date table.
Worked example

Why the month order matters

A chart shows months in alphabetical order: Apr, Aug, Dec, Feb ...

  1. The Month column holds text, which sorts alphabetically.
  2. Select Month, then Column tools → Sort by column → MonthNum.
  3. Now the months run Jan to Dec in every visual.

Answer. A tiny model setting fixes what no chart setting can.

Common mistakes

  • Using a date column from the fact table for time intelligence instead of a date table.
  • Gaps in the date table.
  • Leaving auto date/time on and duplicating dates everywhere.
Try it yourself: Why must a date table have no gaps?

Model answer. Time-intelligence functions assume a continuous run of days; missing days can give wrong 'previous period' results.

Check what you just learned

1. A proper date table has:
  • Only dates that had sales
  • No relationships
  • Times as well as dates
  • One row per day with no gaps (correct)

Continuity is required.

2. To show months Jan to Dec you:
  • Sort Month by MonthNum (correct)
  • Rename them
  • Delete the Month column
  • Use a pie chart

Sorting by another column fixes the order.

Key terms: flip and sort

Fact table
Transactions and the numbers to add up.
Dimension table
Descriptions of the things involved.
Star schema
A fact table surrounded by dimensions.
Cardinality
One-to-many, one-to-one or many-to-many.
Cross-filter direction
Which way filters flow across a relationship.
Date table
One row per day, marked as the date table.
Sort by column
Order one column by another, such as Month by MonthNum.
keyPoints: A date table has one row per day, no gaps, is marked as the date table and is related to the facts.
Sort Month by MonthNum so months are in order.
Hide, name, type and trim the model for users and performance.

modules.title: DAX fundamentals: measures and context
modules.summary: Write your first measures, understand row context and filter context, and use iterators and RELATED.
modules.outcome: You can write measures with SUM, DIVIDE and SUMX, say whether something should be a measure or a calculated column, and explain why a measure gives a different value in every cell of a visual.
modules.intro: DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is the formula language of Power BI. It looks like Excel formulas, and that is both its comfort and its trap: DAX does not work row by row on cells, it works on tables and filters. A single measure such as Total Sales gives a different value in every cell of a matrix, because each cell applies a different filter context. Once that idea clicks, DAX becomes logical. Every lesson here has a live DAX window running on a small star schema, so you see the context at work.

topics.title: Measures: calculations that respond to filters
topics.html:
A measure is a formula that is calculated when a visual is drawn, once for every cell, using whatever filters apply to that cell. Write it once, and it works in every chart, table and matrix.

Formula · The simplest measure

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])

SUM adds the Amount column of the rows that are visible in the current filter context.

One measure, many answers

The same Total Sales measure gives a different value in each row, because each row applies a different filter. Switch between the visuals.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Measure or calculated column?
MeasureCalculated column
CalculatedWhen the visual is drawnWhen the data is refreshed, once per row
StoredNot stored (no memory cost)Stored in the model (uses memory)
Responds to filtersYes, in every cellNo: a fixed value in each row
Use forTotals, ratios, KPIs, anything you aggregateA fixed attribute you slice or filter by (a price band, a flag)

The rule of thumb: if you would put it in the Values area of a visual, it is a measure; if you would put it in Rows, Columns or a slicer, it might be a column. Beginners often create calculated columns for things that should be measures, then wonder why the numbers do not respond to filters.

Build a measure from measures

Measures can use other measures. Define Cost and Margin % by changing the formulas, then show [Margin %].

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Cost = SUM(Sales[Cost])
Margin = [Total Sales] - [Total Cost]
Margin % = DIVIDE([Margin], [Total Sales])
Watch out

Always write ratios with DIVIDE(numerator, denominator), not /. DIVIDE returns BLANK when the denominator is zero or blank, so a cell with no sales shows nothing instead of an error.

Common mistakes

  • A calculated column for a total or ratio: it will not change with filters.
  • Writing a ratio with / and getting divide-by-zero errors.
  • Naming measures 'Measure 1': name them for what they mean.
Try it yourself: Should 'Profit margin %' be a measure or a calculated column?

Model answer. A measure: it is a ratio of totals, so it must be recalculated for every filter context.

Check what you just learned

1. A measure is calculated:
  • Once at refresh
  • When a visual is drawn, for each cell (correct)
  • Never
  • Only for totals

It responds to the filters of each cell.

2. Which is safer for a ratio?
  • a / b
  • a - b
  • DIVIDE(a, b) (correct)
  • a * b

DIVIDE returns BLANK instead of an error when b is zero.
keyPoints: A measure is calculated per cell, using that cell's filters.
Use measures for anything you aggregate and calculated columns for fixed row-level attributes.
Use DIVIDE for ratios.

topics.title: Filter context: why a cell shows what it shows
topics.html:
Every cell of a visual has a filter context: the set of filters applying to it, from the row and column it sits in, from slicers, from page and report filters. The measure is evaluated against only the rows that survive those filters.

Filter context for the cell 'Home / 2025'
Source of the filterFilter applied
Row of the matrixProducts[Category] = Home
Column of the matrixDates[Year] = 2025
A slicer on Stores[Region] set to NorthStores[Region] = North

In that cell, SUM(Sales[Amount]) adds only the sales rows that pass all three filters: Home products, in 2025, in North stores. The relationship does the work: the Products, Dates and Stores filters flow to the Sales table.

See the filter context

In 'Category by year' each cell is a different category and year. The total row and column remove one or both filters.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Orders = COUNTROWS(Sales)
Worked example

Why the total is not the sum of the visible numbers

A matrix shows two categories with sales of 510 and 400, and a total of 910.

  1. The Total row has no category filter, so its context is the whole table.
  2. For a SUM, the total equals the sum of the rows (510 + 400).
  3. For a ratio or an average, the total is computed over everything, not added from the rows above, so it can differ.

Answer. A total is not 'add up the cells'. It is the measure in a smaller (or no) filter context.

Watch out

When a number looks wrong, ask: what is the filter context in this cell? Which filters apply, and which are missing? Nine in ten DAX puzzles are answered this way.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a measure works on one row at a time.
  • Expecting a total row to add up the rows above for ratios and averages.
  • Forgetting that slicers and page filters are part of the context too.
Try it yourself: What is the filter context in the grand-total cell of a matrix with no slicers?

Model answer. None: no filters apply, so the measure sees the whole model.

Check what you just learned

1. The grand total of a ratio measure is:
  • The sum of the cells above
  • The average of the cells
  • Always zero
  • The measure evaluated with no row or column filter (correct)

A total is a smaller filter context.

2. A slicer on Region is part of:
  • The filter context (correct)
  • The row context
  • The model
  • The data type

Slicers add filters.
keyPoints: Each cell's filter context comes from its row, column, slicers and filters.
Filters flow through relationships to the fact table.
A total is the measure with fewer filters, not the sum of the cells.

topics.title: Row context, iterators and RELATED
topics.html:
Filter context decides which rows. Row context is different: it means 'we are on one particular row' and lets a formula read that row's columns. It exists in two places: calculated columns (one row at a time) and iterators, functions ending in X that walk a table row by row.

Aggregators and their iterators
Aggregator (works on one column)Iterator (works row by row on a table)
SUM(Sales[Amount])SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * RELATED(Products[Price]))
AVERAGE(Sales[Qty])AVERAGEX(Sales, ...)
MAX(Sales[Amount])MAXX(Sales, ...)
COUNT(Sales[Qty])COUNTX(Sales, ...)

Use an iterator when the thing to add up is a calculation per row, not a single column. Price times quantity needs both columns on each row, so SUM cannot do it; SUMX can.

SUMX with RELATED

For each Sales row, SUMX multiplies the quantity by the price of the related product. RELATED reads a column from the one side of the relationship. The Difference measure is zero because this small sample has no discounts: a good consistency check.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

List Revenue = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * RELATED(Products[Price]))
Difference = [List Revenue] - [Total Sales]
Definition

RELATED. Reads a column from a table on the 'one' side of a relationship, from a row of the 'many' side. Inside SUMX over Sales, RELATED(Products[Price]) is the price of the product on the current sales row.

Worked example

A measure inside an iterator

Average of the category totals: AVERAGEX(VALUES(Products[Category]), [Total Sales]).

  1. VALUES(Products[Category]) lists the categories in the current context: Stationery and Home.
  2. For each one, [Total Sales] is evaluated for that category (a row context becomes a filter: the context transition).
  3. The results, 510 and 400, are averaged: 455.

Answer. Using a measure inside an iterator re-applies the filter for each row, which is how you average, rank or compare across groups.

Watch out

Iterators over big tables are slow, and an iterator inside an iterator multiplies the work. Iterate over the smallest table that gives the right answer, such as VALUES of a column, not the whole fact table.

Common mistakes

  • Using SUM when a per-row calculation is needed.
  • Forgetting RELATED when reading a dimension column from a fact row.
  • Iterating over a fact table when a dimension would do.
Try it yourself: Write the SUMX for total cost if Cost is price times quantity but the cost per unit is in Products[UnitCost].

Model answer. SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * RELATED(Products[UnitCost]))

Check what you just learned

1. When do you need SUMX rather than SUM?
  • Always
  • When each row needs a calculation from several columns (correct)
  • Never
  • For text

SUM adds one column; SUMX evaluates an expression per row.

2. RELATED returns:
  • A table
  • A filter
  • A column value from the one side of a relationship (correct)
  • A measure

It follows the relationship.
keyPoints: Row context means 'on this row'; iterators (SUMX and friends) create it.
RELATED reads a one-side column from a many-side row.
A measure inside an iterator re-applies filters per row (context transition).

topics.title: Variables and readable measures
topics.html:
VAR stores an intermediate result, and RETURN gives the final answer. Variables make measures easier to read and often faster, because the calculation is done once and reused.

Habits of readable DAX

  • Put each argument of a long function on its own indented line.
  • Name variables for what they hold (sales, last_year), not a and b.
  • Use VAR for a value you use more than once.
  • Comment the why with //.
  • Define small measures and build bigger ones from them.

Variables and IF

VAR holds the value once; RETURN uses it. Change the threshold from 300, or return the number instead of a label.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Size =
    VAR t = [Total Sales]
    RETURN
        IF(t >= 300, "large", "small")
Worked example

A variable that avoids repeating work

Year-on-year growth needs last year's sales twice: once to subtract, once to divide.

  1. Without a variable the same CALCULATE would be written (and evaluated) twice.
  2. With VAR ly = CALCULATE(...), it is evaluated once.
  3. The formula reads: growth is (this − ly) divided by ly.

Answer. Variables turn a puzzle into a sentence.

Watch out

A variable is evaluated where it is defined, in the filter context at that point, not where it is used later. This matters inside CALCULATE and iterators, and is a feature when you understand it.

Common mistakes

  • Meaningless variable names.
  • Defining a variable and never using it.
  • Expecting a variable to change when the context changes later in the formula.

Check what you just learned

1. VAR is used to:
  • Draw charts
  • Filter rows
  • Create a table
  • Store an intermediate value (correct)

It holds a result for reuse.

2. A variable is evaluated:
  • Where it is defined (correct)
  • At the end
  • Never
  • In the report

It keeps that context.

Key terms: flip and sort

Measure
A formula calculated per cell of a visual.
Calculated column
A value stored for every row at refresh.
Filter context
The filters that apply to a cell.
Row context
'On this row' inside an iterator or calculated column.
Iterator
A function ending in X that walks a table row by row.
RELATED
Reads a one-side column from a many-side row.
VAR / RETURN
Store an intermediate value and return the result.
keyPoints: VAR stores a value; RETURN gives the result.
Variables improve readability and performance.
A variable keeps the context of where it was defined.

modules.title: CALCULATE and time intelligence
modules.summary: Change the filter context with CALCULATE, build percent-of-total and share measures, and compare time periods: year to date, last year and growth.
modules.outcome: You can write CALCULATE measures that add, replace or remove filters, build percent of total and share within a group, and calculate year to date, same period last year and year-on-year growth.
modules.intro: If DAX has a single most important function, it is CALCULATE. It evaluates an expression in a modified filter context: 'sales, but for Home only', 'sales, ignoring the category filter', 'sales, for the same period last year'. Nearly every business measure beyond a plain total is CALCULATE in disguise. This module teaches how it works, then applies it to the measures every report needs: percent of total, share within a category, year to date and growth. The practice windows run all of it on a small star schema.

topics.title: CALCULATE: changing the filters
topics.html:
Formula · CALCULATE

CALCULATE( expression, filter1, filter2, ... )

Evaluate the expression after applying the filters to the current context. A filter on a column replaces any existing filter on that same column.

Sales for Home only

The filter on Products[Category] replaces whatever category the cell has, so every row shows Home's sales. Try "Stationery", or use the 'Sales by region' visual.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Home Sales =
    CALCULATE([Total Sales], Products[Category] = "Home")

Look at the result by category: the Stationery row shows 400, not 0. The row's own filter (Category = Stationery) was replaced by CALCULATE's filter (Category = Home). That is the rule: a CALCULATE filter on a column overrides the existing filter on that column, and adds to filters on other columns.

What each filter argument does
ArgumentEffect
Products[Category] = "Home"Replaces the filter on Category with Home
Dates[Year] = 2025Replaces the filter on Year with 2025; other filters stay
Products[Category] IN { "Home", "Stationery" }Replaces Category with the listed values
FILTER(Products, Products[Price] >= 100)Keeps only products meeting a condition on several columns
ALL(Products)Removes every filter on the Products table
KEEPFILTERS(...)Adds the new filter without replacing the old one (intersects)
Worked example

Why the order of filters does not matter

CALCULATE([Total Sales], Dates[Year] = 2025, Products[Category] = "Home")

  1. All filter arguments are evaluated in the original context, then applied together.
  2. Year becomes 2025, Category becomes Home, other filters remain.
  3. Swapping the two filters gives the same answer.

Answer. CALCULATE first works out all the new filters, then evaluates the expression once.

Watch out

A true/false filter such as Products[Category] = "Home" can mention one column (or columns of one table). For conditions that use several tables, or an aggregate such as [Total Sales] > 1000, use FILTER over the right table, because a boolean filter cannot contain a measure.

Common mistakes

  • Expecting CALCULATE to add to an existing filter on the same column: it replaces (use KEEPFILTERS to intersect).
  • Writing a measure inside a boolean filter argument.
  • Forgetting that a row context becomes a filter inside CALCULATE (context transition).
Try it yourself: What does CALCULATE([Total Sales], Stores[Region] = "North") return in the cell for category Home?

Model answer. Sales of Home products in North stores: the Home row filter stays (different column), and Region becomes North.

Check what you just learned

1. CALCULATE([Total Sales], Products[Category] = "Home") in the Stationery row shows:
  • 0
  • Home's sales (correct)
  • Stationery's sales
  • An error

The new filter replaces the row's category filter.

2. Filter arguments of CALCULATE are applied:
  • One at a time, in order
  • Only the first
  • Together, each evaluated in the original context (correct)
  • Randomly

Their order does not matter.
keyPoints: CALCULATE evaluates an expression in a modified filter context.
A filter on a column replaces the existing filter on that column and adds to other columns.
Use FILTER for conditions that need measures or several tables; KEEPFILTERS to intersect.

topics.title: ALL, ALLEXCEPT and percent of total
topics.html:
Removing filters is as useful as adding them. ALL(table) or ALL(column) removes the filters on a table or column; REMOVEFILTERS does the same and reads better; ALLEXCEPT(table, column) removes all filters on a table except those on the named columns.

Formula · Percent of total

Share of Total = DIVIDE( [Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Products)) )

The numerator keeps the row's filters; the denominator removes the Products filters, so it is the total of all products.

Percent of total

Each category's share of all sales. Change ALL(Products) to ALL(Stores) and see what the denominator becomes, or try the 'Category by year' visual.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Share of Total =
    DIVIDE(
        [Total Sales],
        CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Products))
    )
Result by category
CategoryTotal SalesShare of Total
Stationery5100.5604
Home4000.4396
Total9101

Format the measure as a percentage in Power BI (Measure tools → Format → Percentage) and the shares read 56.0% and 44.0%. Notice that the shares add up to 100%, which is a good sanity check.

Worked example

Share within a group

Each product's share of its category (not of all sales).

  1. The denominator must keep the category filter but remove the product filter.
  2. ALLEXCEPT(Products, Products[Category]) removes every Products filter except the category.
  3. DIVIDE([Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLEXCEPT(Products, Products[Category]))).

Answer. With ALL the share would be of everything; with ALLEXCEPT it is of the group.

Share within category

Rows are category then product. The denominator keeps the category and removes the product filter.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Share in Category =
    DIVIDE(
        [Total Sales],
        CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLEXCEPT(Products, Products[Category]))
    )
Watch out

ALL removes filters from the table or column you name, nothing else. If a slicer on Stores should also be ignored in the denominator, you must remove it too: ALL(Products), ALL(Stores) (or use ALLSELECTED in the Desktop, which this practice engine does not run).

Common mistakes

  • Using ALL on the wrong table, so the denominator is not the total you meant.
  • Forgetting to format the result as a percentage.
  • Using ALL on a whole table when only one column should be cleared.
Try it yourself: Which function removes all filters on Products except the Category filter?

Model answer. ALLEXCEPT(Products, Products[Category]).

Check what you just learned

1. The denominator of 'percent of total' usually uses:
  • The same filters as the numerator
  • FILTER
  • SUM only
  • ALL (or REMOVEFILTERS) on the table being split (correct)

It must ignore the row filter.

2. ALLEXCEPT(Products, Products[Category]) keeps:
  • Only the Category filter (correct)
  • No filters
  • All filters
  • Only Product

It removes the others.
keyPoints: ALL, REMOVEFILTERS and ALLEXCEPT remove filters for a measure's denominator.
Percent of total = measure ÷ the same measure with the relevant filters removed.
Check that shares add up to 100%.

topics.title: Time intelligence: year to date and last year
topics.html:
Time intelligence functions need the date table from module 2. They return a set of dates, and CALCULATE uses those dates as a filter.

The core time-intelligence functions
FunctionReturnsExample use
TOTALYTD([m], Dates[Date])The measure from 1 January of the year to the latest date in contextYear-to-date sales
SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Dates[Date])The same dates one year earlierSales last year
DATEADD(Dates[Date], -1, MONTH)The dates shifted by a number of days, months, quarters or yearsSales last month
DATESYTD, DATESMTDDates from the start of the year or month to nowUsed inside CALCULATE
PREVIOUSMONTH, PREVIOUSYEARThe whole previous month or yearLast month's total

Year to date

Each cell is the running total from 1 January to that month. Compare 2024 and 2025 in the 'Month by year' visual, and note the totals column.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Sales YTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], Dates[Date])

Same period last year, and growth

Sales LY looks one year back. 2024 has no earlier year in the data, so its row is blank and hidden, as in Power BI. Growth is the change divided by last year.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Sales LY =
    CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Dates[Date]))
Growth % =
    VAR ly = [Sales LY]
    RETURN DIVIDE([Total Sales] - ly, ly)
Formula · Year-on-year growth

growth = (this period − same period last year) ÷ same period last year

In the sample, 2025 sales were 660 against 250 in 2024: growth is (660 − 250) ÷ 250 = 1.64, or 164%.

Worked example

Why the date table matters

A measure uses SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Sales[Date]) on the fact table's date column.

  1. The fact table has gaps: no row for days without sales.
  2. Time intelligence on a column with gaps gives wrong or empty results.
  3. Using Dates[Date] from a proper, continuous date table fixes it.

Answer. Always pass the date column of the date table, never the fact table's own date column.

Watch out

Compare like with like. Year to date in the middle of a year compared with a full previous year overstates growth. A YTD against the same YTD last year is the fair comparison; SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR applied to a YTD measure does exactly that.

Common mistakes

  • Using the date column of the fact table in time-intelligence functions.
  • A date table with gaps or that does not cover the whole data.
  • Comparing a partial period with a full one.
Try it yourself: What does CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATEADD(Dates[Date], -1, MONTH)) give for March 2025?

Model answer. February 2025's sales (the previous month).

Check what you just learned

1. Which date column do you pass to time-intelligence functions?
  • The fact table's date
  • The date table's Date column (correct)
  • Any text column
  • Year

A continuous, marked date table is required.

2. Year-on-year growth is:
  • this − last
  • this ÷ 100
  • (this − last year's same period) ÷ last year's same period (correct)
  • last year ÷ this

Change as a share of the base.
keyPoints: Time intelligence needs a continuous date table and uses its Date column.
TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and DATEADD return dates that CALCULATE uses as a filter.
Compare the same period last year, not a partial against a full period.

topics.title: Patterns that combine it all
topics.html:
Real reports use a handful of measure patterns again and again. Build them from small measures.

Measure patterns
PatternShape
Percent of totalDIVIDE([m], CALCULATE([m], ALL(dimension)))
Growth versus last yearVAR ly = CALCULATE([m], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Dates[Date])) RETURN DIVIDE([m] - ly, ly)
Running totalTOTALYTD([m], Dates[Date]) or a CALCULATE over dates up to now
Status flagSWITCH(TRUE(), cond1, "A", cond2, "B", "C")
Customers who boughtDISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID])
Average per orderDIVIDE([Total Sales], [Order Count])

A status measure with SWITCH(TRUE())

SWITCH(TRUE(), ...) checks the conditions in order and returns the first that is true. Change the thresholds and the labels.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Dates[Date]))
Status =
    VAR growth = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - [Sales LY], [Sales LY])
    RETURN
        SWITCH(
            TRUE(),
            ISBLANK(growth), "No prior year",
            growth >= 1, "Star",
            growth >= 0, "Steady",
            "Watch"
        )

Habits for a maintainable model of measures

  • Create a separate, empty table named _Measures and keep all measures there.
  • Name measures for the business meaning: Sales LY, not Measure 4.
  • Put the format (currency, percentage, decimals) in the measure, not in each visual.
  • Build ratios from base measures so a change flows everywhere.
  • Write a short comment above any measure that is not obvious.
Worked example

A change flows everywhere

Finance decides that 'sales' should exclude cancelled orders.

  1. Because every other measure is built on [Total Sales], you change that one definition.
  2. Share, growth, YTD and the dashboards all update.
  3. In a model with the logic copied into twenty visuals, you would edit twenty places and miss one.

Answer. Small, well-named base measures are the best investment in a model.

Watch out

Avoid measures that are one gigantic nested formula. If you cannot explain it in a sentence, split it into smaller measures or variables.

Common mistakes

  • Copying the same logic into several measures.
  • Measures scattered across tables.
  • No formatting, so users see 0.5604 where they should see 56%.

Check what you just learned

1. Why build ratios from base measures?
  • It is required
  • It avoids filters
  • It is shorter
  • A change to a base definition flows everywhere (correct)

One definition, many uses.

2. SWITCH(TRUE(), ...) returns:
  • The result of the first true condition (correct)
  • All results
  • The last result
  • A table

Conditions are tested in order.

Key terms: flip and sort

CALCULATE
Evaluates an expression in a modified filter context.
ALL / REMOVEFILTERS
Remove filters from a table or column.
ALLEXCEPT
Remove all filters on a table except the named columns.
KEEPFILTERS
Add a filter without replacing the existing one.
Time intelligence
Functions that shift or accumulate dates.
Year to date
From 1 January to the latest date in context.
Year-on-year growth
Change versus the same period last year, as a share.
keyPoints: A few patterns (share, growth, YTD, status) cover most reports.
Keep measures in one place, named for their meaning, built from small base measures.
Put formatting in the measure; comment what is not obvious.

modules.title: Visuals and report design
modules.summary: Choose the right visual for each question, lay out a report people can read at a glance, and use filters and interactions well.
modules.outcome: You can choose visuals by the question, design a clear page layout, use slicers and filters at the right level, add drill-through and tooltips, and avoid the habits that make reports hard to read.
modules.intro: A report is a conversation between a person and the data. The best model and the cleverest measures are wasted if the page confuses people. This module is about the design decisions that make a report clear: which visual answers which question, where to put things, how interactions should work, and how to make a report accessible and fast. The report canvas is Power BI Desktop's, so this module teaches the decisions and checks your understanding with sorting and writing activities rather than a canvas.

topics.title: Choosing the right visual
topics.html:
Pick the visual by the question, not by what looks interesting.

Question to visual
You want to showUseAvoid
One headline number against a targetCard or KPI visualA gauge with decorative colours
Compare categoriesBar chart (sorted), or clustered columnsA pie with many slices
Change over timeLine chart or area chartA column chart with a truncated axis
Parts of a whole (few parts)A stacked bar, donut or treemap with a handful of parts3D charts
Relationship between two numbersScatter chartTwo separate charts
RankingA sorted bar chart (top N)An unsorted table
Exact valuesTable or matrixA chart that hides the numbers
GeographyMap (when location matters)A map of data that is not about place
Flow or contribution to a changeWaterfallA line chart

Rules of good visual design

  • Bars start at zero; lines may not.
  • Sort categories by value unless they have a natural order.
  • Use colour to highlight one thing, not to decorate everything.
  • Label axes and units; give each visual a title that states the point.
  • Remove clutter: gridlines, borders, shadows, 3D.
  • Limit each page to about six visuals.
Watch out

Pie and donut charts are easy to misread beyond three or four slices because people compare angles poorly. A sorted bar chart almost always communicates the same data better.

Common mistakes

  • A chart type chosen because it looks impressive.
  • Too many colours with no meaning.
  • A table where a chart would show the pattern at once.
Try it yourself: Which visual suits 'which five products sold most?'

Model answer. A sorted horizontal bar chart showing the top five (a Top N filter on the visual).

Check what you just learned

1. Which visual suits change over time?
  • Pie
  • Line (correct)
  • Scatter without time
  • Donut

Lines show trends.

2. Pies are best limited to:
  • Dozens of slices
  • Time series
  • A few parts (correct)
  • Rankings

Many slices are hard to compare.
keyPoints: Choose the visual by the question: cards for numbers, bars for categories, lines for time, scatter for relationships.
Bars start at zero; sort; label; use colour with purpose.
About six visuals per page.

topics.title: Layout, slicers, filters and interactions
topics.html:
A reader should know what the page says within five seconds. Layout does most of the work.

Page layout guidelines

  • Top left first: put the most important number or the page title there; people read from the top left.
  • KPIs across the top, detail below, filters at the left or top.
  • Group related visuals and align them to a grid; equal spacing looks professional and calm.
  • Consistent colours: the same colour always means the same thing across pages.
  • White space is not wasted space.
  • One page, one story: split a crowded page into two.
Filters at three levels
LevelApplies toExample
VisualOne visualShow only the top 5 products in this bar chart
PageEvery visual on the pageThis page covers the current year only
ReportEvery pageExclude test stores

Slicers let the reader filter the page. They are easy to overuse: too many slicers make a page look like a cockpit and invite confusion. Offer the two or three filters people really use (date range, region, category).

Interactions that help readers

  • Cross-filtering: clicking a bar filters the other visuals. Edit interactions (Format → Edit interactions) when a visual should ignore a click.
  • Drill down: move through a hierarchy (Year → Quarter → Month).
  • Drill through: right-click a value to jump to a detail page that is filtered to it.
  • Tooltips: a custom tooltip page can show extra context on hover.
  • Bookmarks and buttons: save a state (a view or filter) and let readers jump between them; good for navigation and for toggling between two charts.
Worked example

Designing for the five-second test

A manager opens the sales report.

  1. Top left: a card showing Sales this year with the growth against last year, in green or red.
  2. Across the top: three more KPI cards (margin %, orders, average order value).
  3. Below: a line chart of sales by month against last year, and a sorted bar of sales by region.
  4. Slicers for Year and Category on the left.

Answer. In five seconds the manager knows whether sales are up or down, by how much, and where to look next.

Watch out

Interactivity can hide information: a report that only makes sense after the right slicer is clicked is a puzzle. Always set sensible defaults, and say on the page what the current filters are.

Common mistakes

  • Twenty visuals on a page.
  • A slicer for every column.
  • Colour meaning different things on different pages.
Try it yourself: What is the difference between drill-down and drill-through?

Model answer. Drill-down goes deeper within the same visual (year to quarter to month); drill-through jumps to a different, filtered detail page.

Check what you just learned

1. A page-level filter applies to:
  • One visual
  • No visuals
  • The whole report
  • Every visual on that page (correct)

Page-level filters affect the page.

2. Drill-through:
  • Jumps to a detail page filtered by the selected value (correct)
  • Goes deeper in the same visual
  • Deletes data
  • Prints

It opens a detail page.
keyPoints: Lay out for the five-second test: key number top left, KPIs across the top, detail below.
Filters apply at visual, page or report level; use few slicers.
Use drill-down, drill-through, tooltips and bookmarks to give detail without clutter.

topics.title: Accessibility, performance and storytelling
topics.html:
A report is only useful if everyone can read it, it loads quickly, and it tells the story.

Accessibility

  • Colour contrast: text and bars must be readable; do not rely on colour alone (add labels or patterns).
  • Alt text for every visual so screen readers describe it.
  • Tab order: set the order in which keyboard users move through visuals.
  • Titles that say something: 'Sales fell in March' rather than 'Sales by month'.
  • Readable font sizes and enough spacing.
  • Use colour-blind-friendly palettes; avoid red/green as the only signal.

Performance

  • Reduce data in Power Query: only needed columns and rows.
  • Use a star schema and one date table.
  • Prefer measures to calculated columns; avoid heavy iterators over large tables.
  • Limit visuals per page, and avoid very high-cardinality fields (an invoice number) in visuals.
  • Use Performance Analyzer (View → Performance analyzer) to see which visual or DAX query is slow.
  • Avoid bi-directional filters and many-to-many relationships unless needed.
Worked example

Reading a slow visual

A page takes eight seconds to load. Performance Analyzer shows one table visual taking six.

  1. The table lists every transaction (200,000 rows).
  2. Replace it with a Top N filter, or a summarised matrix, with drill-through to detail.
  3. Load time drops to two seconds.

Answer. Measure first, then fix the slowest thing.

Storytelling ties it together: a headline in the title, an order that leads the reader (overview, then cause, then detail), and a clear call to action. Use annotation (text boxes) to point at what matters: 'March fell because of one lost customer'.

Watch out

A beautiful report that tells people nothing is decoration. Before building, write the one sentence you want a reader to take away, and design backward from it.

Common mistakes

  • Relying on colour alone to show good and bad.
  • Never testing the report for speed or accessibility.
  • A story that is only visible after ten clicks.
Try it yourself: Name two ways to make a report accessible.

Model answer. Add alt text to visuals, and ensure good contrast and do not use colour as the only signal (also set tab order and use clear titles).

Check what you just learned

1. Alt text helps:
  • Search engines only
  • Screen-reader users understand visuals (correct)
  • Printing
  • Colour

It describes the visual in words.

2. The tool to find slow visuals is:
  • Edit interactions
  • Mark as date table
  • Performance Analyzer (correct)
  • Bookmarks

It times each visual and query.

Key terms: flip and sort

KPI visual
A number compared with a target.
Slicer
An on-page filter control.
Drill-through
Jump to a filtered detail page.
Bookmark
A saved view or filter state.
Alt text
A text description of a visual for screen readers.
Performance Analyzer
A tool that times visuals and queries.
keyPoints: Accessibility: contrast, alt text, tab order, clear titles, not relying on colour alone.
Performance: trim data, use a star schema, prefer measures, use Performance Analyzer.
Lead with the takeaway and annotate what matters.

modules.title: Publish, secure and govern
modules.summary: Share reports through the Power BI Service, schedule refresh, restrict who sees which rows with row-level security, and keep a model trustworthy as it grows.
modules.outcome: You can describe workspaces, apps and refresh, write a row-level security rule as a DAX filter, and list the practices of a governed, certified model.
modules.intro: Building a report is half the job; getting it to the right people, safely and reliably, is the other half. This module covers the Power BI Service: publishing, workspaces and apps, scheduled refresh and gateways, row-level security (RLS) so that each person sees only their own data, and the governance habits that keep a model trusted. These are Service and Desktop features, so they are explained with scenarios and checked with activities; the DAX that defines an RLS rule is a filter expression that you can practise.

topics.title: Publishing, workspaces and apps
topics.html:
When a report is ready in Desktop, publish it to a workspace in the Power BI Service. A workspace is a shared space where a team keeps related reports, models and dashboards.

Sharing choices
OptionWho it suitsNotes
Workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer)The team that builds and maintains contentRoles control who can edit, publish and manage
Share a report with a linkA few colleagues, quicklyRecipients usually need a suitable licence
Publish an appA larger audience of consumersA packaged, read-only version of the content with its own navigation
Embed in Teams or SharePointPeople who work thereReports appear in the tools they already use
Publish to webPublic data onlyAnyone with the link can see it: never for private data
Watch out

'Publish to web' makes a report public to anyone with the link, with no sign-in. Never use it for company data. For internal sharing use workspaces, apps and proper permissions.

Worked example

Separating build from consumption

A finance report is used by 200 managers.

  1. The analysts work in a workspace with Contributor access.
  2. Managers get an app: a polished, read-only copy that updates when the analysts publish a new version.
  3. A mistake in a draft never reaches a manager.

Answer. Apps keep consumers away from half-finished work.

Licensing decides who can publish and share: a free licence for viewing in some situations, Pro or Premium Per User for sharing and collaboration, and Premium or Fabric capacity for large audiences and advanced features. Details and prices change, so check Microsoft's current licensing guide for your organisation.

Common mistakes

  • Publishing to web for convenience.
  • Everyone editing the production report.
  • Sharing individual reports one by one instead of an app.
Try it yourself: Which option gives a large audience a read-only, packaged version of reports?

Model answer. Publish an app from the workspace.

Check what you just learned

1. An app is:
  • A phone
  • A data source
  • A visual
  • A packaged read-only version of workspace content for consumers (correct)

It is a curated release.

2. Publish to web is:
  • Public to anyone with the link (correct)
  • Safe for company data
  • Required
  • Encrypted per user

It exposes data without sign-in.
keyPoints: Publish from Desktop to a workspace; share with roles, links or an app.
Use apps for large audiences and separate development from production.
Never use Publish to web for private data.

topics.title: Refresh, gateways and keeping data current
topics.html:
Imported data is a snapshot. Scheduled refresh reloads it on a timetable so reports stay current.

Refresh basics
TopicWhat to know
Scheduled refreshSet in the Service on the semantic model: choose the days and times; a limited number of refreshes a day on shared capacity, more on Premium
On-premises sourcesNeed an on-premises data gateway that securely connects the Service to a database or file inside your network
Cloud sourcesConnect directly with stored credentials
Incremental refreshReload only recent partitions of a large table instead of everything
FailuresThe owner is emailed; check credentials, gateway status, changed column names or a source that was moved

A reliable refresh

  • Use a service account or organisational credential, not one person's password.
  • Keep the gateway on a reliable always-on machine, and install it as a standard (not personal) gateway for shared use.
  • Schedule refresh after the source's own overnight load completes.
  • Monitor failures and set alerts.
  • Do not rename or remove source columns without updating the query.
Worked example

A morning report that is stale

Managers complain that the 8 a.m. report shows yesterday's data.

  1. The source database finishes its overnight load at 6:30.
  2. The refresh was scheduled at 5:00, before the load.
  3. Move the refresh to 7:00: the report is current at 8:00.

Answer. Align refresh with when the source is ready.

Watch out

A report's 'last refreshed' time is easy to forget. Show it on the page, so readers know how old the numbers are.

Common mistakes

  • Refreshing before the source has finished updating.
  • Tying refresh to one employee's personal credentials.
  • A gateway on a laptop that is switched off at night.
Try it yourself: Why does an on-premises database need a gateway?

Model answer. The Power BI Service is in the cloud; the gateway is a secure bridge so it can reach data inside your own network.

Check what you just learned

1. Why schedule refresh after the source's overnight load?
  • It is cheaper
  • So the report reflects the finished data (correct)
  • Power BI requires it
  • To skip it

Refresh too early reloads old data.

2. A gateway is needed for:
  • Cloud files only
  • Charts
  • Data sources inside your own network (correct)
  • Colours

It bridges the cloud and on-premises.
keyPoints: Scheduled refresh keeps imported data current; time it after the source loads.
On-premises sources need a gateway.
Use shared credentials, monitor failures and show the last-refreshed time.

topics.title: Row-level security and governance
topics.html:
Row-level security (RLS) restricts which rows of data each person sees, with one report and one model. You define roles, each with a DAX filter expression on a table, and assign people to roles in the Service.

RLS examples
RoleFilter expression on a tableEffect
North managersStores[Region] = "North"Only North's stores, and so only their sales (the filter flows to Sales)
Product teamProducts[Category] IN { "Home", "Stationery" }Only those categories
Each manager (dynamic)Stores[ManagerEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()Each user sees their own stores: one role for everyone

What a role would see

An RLS rule is a filter on a dimension table. This measure shows the sales a North-only role would see: it applies the same filter. Compare with the unfiltered total.

Tables: Products, Stores, Sales, Dates. Starting formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
North Role Sales =
    CALCULATE([Total Sales], Stores[Region] = "North")

The filter flows through the relationship exactly as in the DAX you have written: a rule on Stores restricts Sales. In the Service you test a role with View as. Desktop lets you define roles (Modeling → Manage roles) and test them with View as.

Watch out

RLS only protects data if people access it through the Service with their own identity, and if they are not workspace Admins, Members or Contributors (those roles can see all the data). Test every role, and never rely on hiding a visual as security.

Governance habits

  • Certify and promote trusted semantic models, so people reuse them instead of building their own copies.
  • Document: descriptions on tables, columns and measures.
  • Sensitivity labels classify data (for example Confidential) and travel with it.
  • Lineage and impact analysis show which reports depend on a model before you change it.
  • Naming standards and version control for the model files.
  • Least privilege: give people the lowest access that lets them do their job.
Worked example

One model, many audiences

A regional sales model serves four regional managers and a head-office team.

  1. Four RLS roles, one per region, each with a filter on Stores[Region].
  2. A head-office role with no filter.
  3. One report, one refresh, and each manager sees only their region.

Answer. RLS replaces four copies of the report with one.

Common mistakes

  • Hiding a visual and calling it security.
  • Testing RLS only as the report author (an admin sees everything).
  • Building a new model for every report.
Try it yourself: Write an RLS filter so each manager sees only their stores, if Stores has a ManagerEmail column.

Model answer. Stores[ManagerEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME() (a dynamic rule: one role for all managers).

Check what you just learned

1. An RLS rule is:
  • A chart
  • A slicer
  • A refresh schedule
  • A DAX filter expression on a table (correct)

It filters a table for a role.

2. Who can bypass RLS?
  • Workspace Admins, Members and Contributors (correct)
  • Viewers
  • Nobody
  • App users

Edit-level roles see all data.

Key terms: flip and sort

Workspace
A shared space for related content.
App
A packaged, read-only release of workspace content.
Scheduled refresh
Reloading imported data on a timetable.
Gateway
A secure bridge to on-premises data.
Row-level security
Restricting which rows a person sees.
Sensitivity label
A classification that travels with data.
Certified model
A model endorsed as trustworthy for reuse.
keyPoints: RLS uses DAX filter expressions on tables, per role, with one model.
Test with View as; workspace Admins, Members and Contributors bypass RLS.
Govern with certified models, documentation, sensitivity labels and least privilege.

capstone.title: Final project: the executive scorecard and a report design brief
capstone.summary: Write the scorecard measure that combines growth and margin, write the design brief for the report, and pass the final assessment.
capstone.intro: You can now explain the Power BI workflow, design a star-schema model with a date table, write measures with SUMX, CALCULATE and time intelligence, and make design and sharing decisions. In this final project you play the BI developer for Kiran Stores. First build the Scorecard measure in the DAX lab: it gives each region and year one status word using growth against last year and margin. Then, in the document lab, write a one-page report design brief with the audience, the question, the visuals, the refresh and the row-level security. Finally take the assessment, which covers the whole course.
